title: The Fall of Kiev
subtitle: Withdrawal across the Dnieper and the first days of occupation
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: Kiev fell while the pocket battle continued. Diaries and orders reveal selective evacuation, household survival, army involvement in persecution and the separate chronology of Soviet demolitions and German crimes.
body:
The army leaves, the city remains

On 19 September 1941, German troops entered Kiev (Kyiv) after the Soviet withdrawal. East of the Dnieper, the defenders were still caught within a larger encirclement. Inside the city, inhabitants were searching for food and water, protecting their homes and trying to discover what the new authorities would require. The army had left; the city had not emptied. Its fall therefore began two histories that ran alongside one another: the continuing destruction of Soviet military formations and the establishment of German power over the people who remained. [1][2]a

The German junction east of Kiev had already made a Dnieper crossing insufficient for escape. The 37th Army could leave the city and still remain within the larger pocket, while other formations attempted breakouts farther east. Capturing Kiev and destroying the encircled armies were related operations with different endpoints. The inhabitants entered occupation while resistance beyond the river continued.

Kiev’s inhabitants also entered the day from unequal positions. Some families had left with evacuated institutions, some men had been mobilised, and others remained because they lacked transport, had responsibilities they could not abandon or did not expect occupation to threaten them in the same way. The population visible to the entering Germans was consequently not a representative sample of the prewar city. Evacuation had altered its social composition before the first occupation order appeared. The experiences of those left behind must be understood through that selection as well as through the policies the Germans introduced.

Withdrawal through the Dnieper crossings

The written permission to abandon Kiev was issued at 23.40 on 17 September. It authorised withdrawal to the eastern bank of the Dnieper and required the removal of weapons from the fortified region where possible. Equipment that could not be evacuated was to be destroyed, along with bridges and other military installations. The order ended the demand to retain the city, but its implementation required an army already weakened by prolonged fighting to move through a restricted number of crossings. The same installations that had supported the defence now became bottlenecks through which the defenders had to pass.[3]

The 37th Army’s warning, forwarded to higher command on 17 September, described the immediate danger. German pressure had broken parts of its western defence, while attacks east of the river threatened the crossings from behind. Contact with neighbouring formations was missing, reserves were exhausted and transport was accumulating in Kiev and Darnytsia. These were connected failures. A bridge could remain physically intact while the roads leading away from it became unsafe. Moving another column across would not solve the problem if that column then became trapped in congestion on the eastern bank.[3]b

The army was being asked to preserve fighting power while denying useful infrastructure to its pursuers. Those aims could conflict. Guns needed towing vehicles or horses, ammunition required carrying capacity, and wounded men could not necessarily move at the pace of the infantry. Delaying a demolition might allow more Soviet troops to cross but increase the risk that the Germans would seize the bridge. Advancing it might protect the retreating main body while abandoning stragglers. The written order supplied a principle; local commanders still had to judge timing amid incomplete information and changing pressure.

The river’s scale made those decisions especially consequential. Kiev’s western districts stood across a major water barrier from Darnytsia and the roads towards Boryspil and Brovary. A movement out of the city required more than reaching the waterfront. Formations had to preserve enough organisation to use the approaches, cross and then continue towards their assigned destinations. Military transport did not arrive in a single uniform stream. Headquarters vehicles, artillery teams, infantry and supply columns had different speeds and stopping requirements. When those streams mixed under pressure, the obstruction of one could immobilise several others.

The departure took place under the pressure of German infantry armies as well as the distant armoured barrier. The 6th Army under Walter von Reichenau operated against Kiev, and the XXIX Army Corps under Hans von Obstfelder became central to the city’s initial occupation. The capture should therefore not be imagined as the same panzer spearheads simply driving back from their junction to take the city. Mobile formations and infantry were performing related but different tasks: the former had interrupted the Soviet routes east, while the latter pressed and occupied the positions being abandoned.[4][1]c

Residents saw soldiers leaving, vehicles moving and installations being destroyed without knowing the army’s intended destinations or which crossings remained usable. Headquarters possessed planned routes but often lacked its units’ current positions. Reading these accounts together connects the immediate effects in Kiev with a withdrawal whose wider course was becoming uncertain even to the officers directing it.

A soldier sheltered on Andriivskyi Descent

On 25 September, Iryna Khoroshunova recalled a young Soviet soldier running up Andriivskyi Descent as the Germans entered six days earlier. Women took him inside, gave him bread and found civilian clothes. He left that evening; her account does not establish his later fate. The encounter brought a withdrawing army into a household through the needs of one man. For a short time, his protection depended on people outside his unit, while the women assumed the risk of helping someone the occupying authorities might seek. This is a recollection recorded several days afterward, rather than an entry written during the encounter.[5]d

The city that could not evacuate itself

Historian Dmytro Malakov’s study of the first occupation days emphasises the selective character of evacuation. Skilled workers and technical staff from important enterprises, officials, prominent cultural figures and their families had opportunities linked to institutional priorities. Their departure emptied particular buildings and neighbourhoods more thoroughly than others. This was not a comprehensive evacuation of the civilian population. The distinction matters because remaining in Kiev cannot be treated as a single political choice. Access to a train, a recognised workplace assignment or a family connection could shape the outcome as decisively as a person’s preference.[6]

Even institutional employment did not assure evacuation. Elena Zinkevych and Michelle Assay’s research identifies the absence of an official evacuation for the Kiev Conservatoire, leaving many teachers and students in the occupied city. The available chapter abstract establishes this point without supplying the full analysis. It qualifies any image of a uniformly evacuated cultural elite. Professional standing mattered alongside the resources and decisions of particular institutions, and did not always provide an organised way out.[7]e

Households also faced decisions that could not be solved through an institutional order. Taking an elderly relative required space, assistance and a destination; leaving that person behind could be unacceptable even when departure was possible for someone younger. Packing possessions consumed time but might preserve the means to survive elsewhere. Information about transport could change faster than a family could act on it. These are not reasons to assume that everyone understood the danger and freely chose to remain. They explain why opportunity, knowledge and responsibility had to coincide before evacuation became a real option.

On 19 September, Anatolii Pavliuk saw people carrying flour and unbaked dough from bakeries. Regular distribution was breaking down as the Soviet authorities withdrew. Reaching food physically present in a building required a way to carry it, sometimes little more than a person’s hands. His observation shows inhabitants securing provisions during that transition; it cannot establish the quantity left in Kiev or the circumstances of every person taking it.[8]f

The distinction between food physically present and food available through a dependable system was crucial. A family might acquire something during the transition and still have no means of replacing it. Flour required water, fuel and a place to prepare it. A shop could contain goods while lacking staff, authorisation or a secure means of opening. Money retained its physical form even when there was little that could be bought with it. The arrival of a new administration did not automatically restore those relationships. Civilian survival depended on practical exchanges that military possession of the streets did not itself provide.

Protecting the windows with bedding

Nina Herasymova used a mattress and pillows to cover her windows on 18 September, hoping to stop flying glass. Her diary set the precaution beside troop movements and the loss of water and radio service. The next day brought an unfamiliar quiet and German motorcyclists. Published selections, translated into Ukrainian from her Russian notebooks, preserve these changes from inside a household. Bedding could not control the battle or the demolitions, but it offered something her family could do to reduce danger in its own rooms.[9]g

Occupation becomes a system of authority

German occupation began with military institutions already present behind the advancing troops. Berkhoff identifies Alfred von Puttkammer, commander of Rear Army Area 585, as the first city commander, followed on 23 September by Kurt Eberhard of Field Command 175. He also stresses uncertainty about the precise transfer of authority between army and army-group rear commands. The uncertainty does not imply an absence of German authority. It shows overlapping institutions whose responsibilities cannot be reduced to a single official’s title. An advance detachment of Paul Blobel’s Sonderkommando 4a arrived on 19 September, bringing the security-police apparatus into the city from the beginning.[4]

For residents, authority appeared through armed men, notices, requisitions and requirements to register. Malakov records orders appearing on 21 September concerning registration, work, weapons and goods taken during the transition. These dates should remain separate from the entry on 19 September. Occupation did not arrive as a fully understood set of rules at one instant; its demands accumulated over the following days. The threat of severe punishment made uncertainty especially dangerous. A person might need to report to an office or surrender an item without knowing whether the instruction would remain the same the next morning.[6]

Registration was more than a means of restoring ordinary administration. It made people and institutions legible to an occupying power: where someone lived, what work they had performed and what category the authorities assigned to them could determine their treatment. A workplace list could help reopen an essential service, but it could also identify people for compulsory labour or persecution. The same act of providing information could therefore carry different consequences for different residents. The administrative language of order should not conceal the coercion behind it or the unequal status built into the occupation.

Jewish residents were subjected to persecution before the explosions of 24 September. German military units imposed hazardous forced labour, and on 22 September XXIX Army Corps commander Hans von Obstfelder ordered the arrest of the city’s Jewish men. Berkhoff documents these acts alongside the arrival of Blobel’s security-police detachment. They identify army participation in the initial persecution rather than leaving responsibility with an undefined atmosphere of occupation. Their chronology also defeats the later claim that the fires originated anti-Jewish violence. The occupiers had already targeted Jews when the explosions gave them another pretext. [4]h

Other residents could experience uncertainty without facing the same immediate danger. Ukrainian hopes for political change, memories of Soviet repression and ordinary relief that bombardment had paused did not create a common response to the Germans. Nor did a gesture of welcome establish consent to the regime that followed. People interpreted the arrival through different experiences and incomplete information. The historian should resist converting selected spectators into the voice of the city. Occupation imposed a hierarchy of power and vulnerability even where residents had initially imagined that it might bring something else.

Army commands, security-police units and local auxiliaries brought different powers into the city. Labour requisitions, building seizures, arrests and the delivery of instructions into neighbourhoods connected their work. Cooperation enabled persecution, while orders and reports identify particular responsibilities. The existence of several institutions should neither obscure their documented actions nor make the conduct of every person attached to them identical.

The battle continues beyond the city

While occupation authorities established themselves in Kiev, Soviet headquarters were still trying to locate the armies east of it. A General Staff conversation dated 19 September records an intercepted radio message from the 5th Army’s area around Pyriatyn and Krucha asking for help before contact ceased. The higher headquarters did not possess a clear picture of Kirponos, Potapov or the neighbouring commands. This is the military counterpoint to the city’s capture: the Germans could announce possession of Kiev while Soviet officers were still searching for information about forces that had left it or fought elsewhere within the pocket.[3]

The same exchange reveals that technical connection and useful communication were not identical. Calls to the 38th Army sometimes reached signals personnel who could not answer operational questions; by the time a commander or staff officer was brought to the equipment, the connection had failed. An officer sent by aircraft had not returned when the report was made. These details explain why headquarters could not simply consult a map and redirect every formation. The map itself depended on reports that were late, incomplete or missing. Even where communications equipment functioned briefly, the right person and the necessary information might not be available together.[3]i

Supply efforts continued into the following day. On 20 September, the General Staff pressed the Southwestern Direction to send fuel and ammunition by air to Kirponos’s forces, particularly to Fyodor Kostenko’s 26th Army. It reported that substantial equipment could not be moved because fuel was lacking. The planned flights had not all departed, and the small number expected was judged inadequate. This was an attempt to preserve movement and fighting capacity within the pocket, not evidence of a successful air bridge. The difference between a dispatch order and a completed delivery remained decisive.[3]

The request included using combat aircraft if necessary. That instruction demonstrates the urgency but also the limitations of improvisation. An aircraft assigned to carry supplies could not perform its usual mission at the same time, and the load it could deliver still had to reach the intended troops. Fuel was especially consequential because vehicles without it could become fixed stores of weapons and equipment rather than means of escape. Abandoning those vehicles might allow some men to move, but it would reduce the material strength with which they could continue fighting after a breakout.

Outside the main pocket, Belov’s group was still fighting around Romny. A report conveyed on 20 September described the positions reached after hard fighting on the previous day and noted the arrival or concentration of additional formations. The German eastern flank therefore remained an active front while Kiev was being occupied. This continued resistance did not reverse the encirclement, but it constrained the encircling forces and required them to retain troops facing outward. The fall of the city should not be allowed to flatten these simultaneous operations into an image of universal Soviet surrender.[3]j

Medical services, transport offices and supply personnel were caught in the same fragmentation as combat units. Their loss mattered because armies depended on specialised work that could not be recreated merely by collecting survivors. A driver who escaped without his vehicle, a surgeon separated from equipment or a signals operator without a functioning network could still serve again, but the immediate organisation had been damaged. The Soviet defeat therefore involved more than the number of riflemen removed from the line. It broke relationships between people, matériel and institutions that had made large-scale resistance possible.

The General Staff responded to the information crisis by sending liaison officers as well as demanding reports. On 20 September it announced that Captain Reznik and Senior Lieutenant Saltykov were flying from Moscow to Kharkov for assignment to the 38th Army. Theatre headquarters was told to meet them, provide a map, explain the situation and send them onward by car. Their mission was to remain with the army and report by whatever means were available. This was a concrete attempt to reconnect levels of command after ordinary channels had proved insufficient. It also required scarce aircraft and vehicles for the movement of two officers whose principal resource was their ability to carry reliable information.[3]

Theatre staff protested that their available communication lines could not carry every requested form of report while replacing the functions of the missing front headquarters. Encryption introduced further delay. The exchange exposes an administrative limit to military control: demanding more information could overload the system needed to transmit it. As Kiev entered occupation, Soviet command was still trying to determine which reports were essential and how to obtain them in time to influence the fighting.[3]k

Destruction after the entry

The explosions that devastated central Kiev began on 24 September, five days after the German entry. Berkhoff identifies Red Army engineers and NKVD personnel as responsible for planting explosives; the blasts and ensuing fires also endangered the city’s inhabitants. These events must be distinguished from the demolitions accompanying the withdrawal and from German decisions to murder Jews. The order of 17 September to deny military resources does not identify every later device or its target. Nor does evidence that Soviet personnel planted explosives establish collective responsibility among the people whom the Germans subsequently blamed. [4]

Pavliuk’s entry of 26 September described the blast two days earlier and fires spreading through central Kiev, while remaining uncertain about the first explosion’s exact location. Damaged water service increased the danger to homes. His entries also recorded accusations: on 26 September he linked arrests of Jews to sabotage, and on 28 September he repeated fears of further sabotage by Jews. Those passages preserve rumours and interpretations circulating in the occupied city. They do not establish Jewish responsibility for the Soviet explosives.[8]

German authorities turned the Soviet demolitions into an accusation against Jews collectively. That was the perpetrators’ chosen pretext. Persecution before 24 September shows that the policy had not begun as an answer to the fires. The occupation’s institutions were already classifying, arresting and exploiting people; the explosions supplied a public justification for further violence. Victory and Catastrophe follows the organisation of the massacre that came next.[2]l

Responsibility for destroying infrastructure and responsibility for murdering civilians are distinct questions. Identifying Soviet demolition work does not transfer responsibility for German crimes to the people targeted by them. Identifying German persecution does not erase the suffering caused to residents by the destruction of water, power or shelter during the Soviet withdrawal. An evidence-led account can address both without treating them as equivalent policies or using one to excuse the other. The city’s inhabitants experienced consequences from decisions made by several institutions, but those institutions retained responsibility for their own actions.

What the capture accomplished

Kiev’s fall removed a major defended position from the German army’s immediate front and gave the occupiers control of an important city. It did not restore the bridges, eliminate Soviet resistance throughout the pocket or provide a functioning urban economy ready to serve German needs. The victory therefore created tasks as well as opportunities: engineers, guards, administrative staffs and transport services had to operate in a damaged environment while the armies continued fighting. German military success and the city’s civilian crisis were connected through the use of the same roads, buildings, labour and supplies.

Leaving Kiev offered the 37th Army a chance to attempt escape, but the permission came after the larger routes had been cut. The city’s residents faced a different loss: armed authority now rested with an occupier already separating, arresting and exploiting people according to persecutory categories. The diaries preserve acts of shelter, improvisation and assistance within that transition. They also preserve uncertainty about what came next. The Destruction of the Pocket follows the soldiers beyond the city, where continued fighting was giving way to escape, disappearance and mass captivity.

sourceMethod: Lettered notes retain detailed references, access limits and qualifications; numbered citations lead to the sources below. Retrospective accounts, translated extracts and abstracts are identified where used. Later events retain their own dates. The dated atlas has separate feature sources and precision notes.
